The Gītā itself names plural paths by temperament (3.3; 13.24–25) and grades them by capacity (6.3; 12.8–11), so all schools agree the four yogas are taught; which is the final, direct means of liberation is not yet reconciled.

The Gītā reconciles the two itself: action is the means for one ascending and quiescence for one ascended (6.3), true renunciation is acting without depending on the fruit (6.1), saṃnyāsa and tyāga are redefined (18.2), and Sāṃkhya and Yoga are one in result (5.4–5).

In the narrative Yudhiṣṭhira is persuaded: renunciation proper belongs to its stage of life, and inner non-possession ('na mama') is possible while ruling; the Mokṣadharma then teaches liberation to the ruling king.

The text itself reconciles them: both views are true and both, practised according to scripture, lead to the highest goal (12.289.7–8); the Gītā says those who see Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one see (5.4–5); the Nārāyaṇīya calls them limbs of one another (12.336.76).
The Mokṣadharma itself frames the answer as 'many as individuals, one as their source' (12.338.3), a difference of standpoint (the individuals vs their ground).

The Gītā gives five causes of every action — the body, the agent, the instruments, the activities and daiva (18.14) — so each position names one causal factor from its own standpoint; Bhīṣma's seed-and-field image joins fate and effort (13.6.7).
The text itself says Jābāli spoke only as a means to bring Rāma back, knowing well the coming and going of the world (Vasiṣṭha, 2.110.1); the reconciliation concerns Jābāli's intention only.
The epic states that Rudra and Nārāyaṇa are one being made twofold, manifest in all actions (12.328.24), so the praises of each are read as the one being praised under two forms.
